CHAPTER 2.4 · LEARNING AREA 2

CHAPTER 2.4 · LEARNING AREA 2 · FEBRUARY · MARCH

Percentages

“Everything 30% cheaper!”, “Battery 35% charged”, “19% VAT”: you meet percentages everywhere. One per cent is one hundredth. You learn the three basic problems of percentages, calculate with discounts and VAT, understand the difference between “increase by” and “increase to” and read percentages in charts and newspapers critically.

16 LESSONS4 UNITS1 LAB
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • distinguish and calculate the base value, the percentage amount and the percentage rate
  • calculate discounts and VAT, also with a spreadsheet
  • calculate with the multiplier: “an increase by 20%” is “an increase to 120%”
  • work back from the new value to the base value
  • show proportions in bar charts and pie charts and read percentages critically
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

What percentage is $\tfrac14$?

$\tfrac14 = \tfrac{25}{100} = 25\%$

What is 1% of €300?

One hundredth: €3.

Write 0.07 as a percentage.

$0.07 = \tfrac{7}{100} = 7\%$

What is 10% of 70?

One tenth: 7.

  • On which item do you save more money?
  • On which is the price reduction in per cent bigger?

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Percentages and the basic problems

“Per cent” comes from the Italian per cento, “of a hundred”. $35\%$ means: 35 out of 100, i.e. $\tfrac{35}{100} = 0.35$. With percentages you can compare proportions well, even if the wholes are of different sizes.

Every percentage problem has three quantities: the whole, the proportion in per cent and the part that belongs to this proportion. You know two of them; the third is what you are looking for.

KEY POINT · THE BASIC PROBLEMS

$1\% = \tfrac{1}{100} = 0.01$. The base value $G$ is the whole (100%), the percentage rate $p\%$ is the proportion, the percentage amount $W$ is the part.

Percentage amount required: $\;W = p\% \cdot G$   ·   Percentage rate required: $\;p\% = \dfrac{W}{G}$   ·   Base value required: $\;G = \dfrac{W}{p\%}$

It also works with the unitary method: what is 1%, and then what is $p\%$?

Memory aid: The three formulas are one formula, rearranged as in chapter 2.3.

Over 100% is possible: 120% of 50 is 60. The part is then bigger than the whole, for example after a price rise.

INTERACTIVE · HUNDRED SQUARE AND PERCENTAGE BAR
EXAMPLE 1 · PERCENTAGE AMOUNT AND PERCENTAGE RATE

a) What is 35% of €80?   b) 12 out of 30 pupils come by bike. What percentage is that?

a) $W = 0.35 \cdot €80 = €28$

b) $p\% = \tfrac{12}{30} = 0.4 = 40\%$ €28 · 40%

EXAMPLE 2 · BASE VALUE

15% of the pocket money is €9. How much is the whole pocket money?

Formula: $G = \tfrac{€9}{0.15} = €60$. Unitary method: 15% is €9, 1% is €0.60, 100% is €60.

The pocket money is €60.

EXERCISES

Calculate: a) 20% of €45   b) 3% of 1200 m   c) 75% of 64   d) 120% of 50

a) €9   b) 36 m   c) 48   d) 60

What percentage is a) 6 out of 24   b) 18 out of 120   c) 45 out of 36?

a) 25%   b) 15%   c) 125%

Calculate the base value: a) 30% is 12 kg   b) 8% is €20   c) 150% is 75

a) 40 kg   b) €250   c) 50

Of the 640 pupils at a school, 35% come by bus and 15% by bike. How many is that in each case? How many come to school in other ways?

Bus: $0.35 \cdot 640 = 224$, bike: $0.15 \cdot 640 = 96$. Other ways: $640 - 320 = 320$, i.e. half.

In your head: 10% and 1% are easy. Use them to calculate 11% of 300 and 9% of 300. Explain your method.

10% of 300 is 30, 1% is 3. 11% is $30 + 3 = 33$, 9% is $30 - 3 = 27$.

TEST YOURSELF!

What is 25% of 60?

A quarter: 15.

What percentage is 9 out of 36?

$\tfrac{9}{36} = \tfrac14 = 25\%$

20% is 14. What is the base value?

$14 \div 0.2 = 70$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Percentages in everyday life

In the sale you save 25% of €80 on the jacket, i.e. €20. On the trousers you save €15 of €60, which is also 25%. The proportion is the same, but you save more money on the jacket, because the base value is bigger.

KEY POINT · DISCOUNT AND VAT

A discount is a price reduction. The new price is the old price minus the discount.

In Germany most goods carry VAT (value added tax) of 19%, many foods 7%. The price without tax is called the net price, the price with tax the gross price: $\;\text{gross} = \text{net} + 19\%\text{ of net}$.

In a spreadsheet a formula recalculates for every row, for example =B2*C2 for 20% of B2 if C2 contains “20%”.

Spreadsheet: If you drag a formula down, it adapts: =B2*C2 becomes =B3*C3 in the next row.

THIS IS WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE IN A SPREADSHEET
ABCDE
1ItemPriceDiscountReductionNew price
2Jacket€80.0025%=B2*C2 → €20.00=B2-D2 → €60.00
3Shoes€65.0020%€13.00€52.00

EXAMPLE 3 · DISCOUNT

Shoes cost €65. In the sale there is a 20% discount. How much do they cost now?

Discount: $0.2 \cdot €65 = €13$. New price: $€65 - €13$.

The shoes cost €52.

EXAMPLE 4 · VAT

A bicycle costs €250 net. What is the gross price with 19% VAT?

Tax: $0.19 \cdot €250 = €47.50$. Gross: $€250 + €47.50$.

The gross price is €297.50.

EXERCISES

A rucksack costs €45. There is a 30% discount. Calculate the reduction and the new price.

Reduction €13.50, new price €31.50.

A repair costs €120 net. Calculate the VAT (19%) and the gross price.

Tax €22.80, gross €142.80.

A loaf of bread costs €3.50 net. The reduced tax rate of 7% applies to bread. How much does it cost with tax? How much more would it be with 19%?

With 7%: $3.50 + 0.245 \approx €3.75$. With 19%: $3.50 + 0.665 \approx €4.17$, so about €0.42 more.

In the table above, B5 contains a price of €120 and C5 a discount of 15%. Which formulas belong in D5 and E5? Which values appear?

D5: =B5*C5 → €18.00. E5: =B5-D5 → €102.00.

In a class of 28 pupils, 7 have no brothers or sisters. What percentage is that? How many would it be with the same proportion at a school with 840 pupils?

$\tfrac{7}{28} = 25\%$. At the school: $0.25 \cdot 840 = 210$.

TEST YOURSELF!

A game costs €40. With a 15% discount it costs …

$40 - 6 = €34$

How much VAT (19%) is added to a net price of €100?

€19

A price of €48 is reduced by €12. By what percentage?

$\tfrac{12}{48} = 25\%$

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3“Increase by” and “increase to”

Ten per cent twice: €100 plus 10% is €110. 10% less than that is $110 - 11 = €99$. The price is not €100 again! The second 10% refers to a different base value. With a multiplier you see such things at once.

KEY POINT · CALCULATING WITH THE MULTIPLIER

An increase by $p\%$ is an increase to $(100 + p)\%$. The new value is $\;G \cdot \left(1 + \tfrac{p}{100}\right)$. Example: by 20% → multiplier $1.2$.

A decrease by $p\%$ is a decrease to $(100 - p)\%$. The new value is $\;G \cdot \left(1 - \tfrac{p}{100}\right)$. Example: by 20% → multiplier $0.8$.

Working back: base value $=$ new value $\div$ multiplier. Several changes: the multipliers are multiplied together.

Typical mistake: After a 20% discount something costs €360. The old price is not $360 + 20\%$, because the 20% refers to the old price.

Doubling is an increase by 100%, i.e. to 200%.

INTERACTIVE · BEFORE AND AFTER

Set the change. Then tap “Then back by the same percentage”.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE RENT GOES UP

A rent of €600 rises by 4%. What is the new rent?

An increase by 4% is an increase to 104%, multiplier $1.04$.

$1.04 \cdot €600 = €624$

EXAMPLE 6 · WORKING BACK

After a 20% discount a bicycle costs €360. How much did it cost before?

€360 is 80% of the old price: multiplier $0.8$. Old price: $€360 \div 0.8$.

The bicycle cost €450, not $360 \cdot 1.2 = €432$.

EXERCISES

Give the multiplier: a) 15% more   b) 8% less   c) to 130%   d) 100% more   e) 50% less

a) $1.15$   b) $0.92$   c) $1.3$   d) $2$   e) $0.5$

a) €250 plus 12%   b) 80 kg minus 35%   c) 1.5 ℓ plus 20%

a) $1.12 \cdot 250 = €280$   b) $0.65 \cdot 80 = 52$ kg   c) $1.2 \cdot 1.5 = 1.8$ ℓ

After a price rise of 25% a cinema ticket costs €15. How much did it cost before?

$15 \div 1.25 = €12$

A shop raises a price by 20% and then gives a 20% discount. A customer says: “That’s just the old price.” Is he right?

No. $1.2 \cdot 0.8 = 0.96$: afterwards the price is 4% lower than at the start.

A town has 50,000 inhabitants. The number grows by 2% each year for two years. How many inhabitants does it have then? Is that the same as growth of 4%?

$50{,}000 \cdot 1.02 \cdot 1.02 = 52{,}020$. With 4% it would be 52,000. Almost the same, but not quite: in the second year the new inhabitants grow as well.

TEST YOURSELF!

€200 rises by 15%. New value?

$1.15 \cdot 200 = €230$

€75 falls by 20%. New value?

$0.8 \cdot 75 = €60$

After a 25% discount something costs €60. How much did it cost before?

$60 \div 0.75 = €80$

UNIT 44 LESSONS

4Bar charts and pie charts

In the election for class representative Anna gets 12 out of 30 votes, which is 40%. In the pie chart she gets 40% of the circle, i.e. 40% of 360°. How big is this angle?

KEY POINT · PROPORTIONS IN A CHART

In a bar chart the height of a bar is proportional to the value. It is good for comparing.

In a pie chart the whole circle is 100%. A proportion of $p\%$ gets the angle $\;p \cdot 3.6^\circ$, because $1\% \text{ of } 360^\circ = 3.6^\circ$. It shows parts of a whole.

Read critically: a percentage of what? If a proportion rises from 20% to 25%, that is 5 percentage points more, but 25% more.

Check: All the proportions together make 100%, all the angles together 360°.

Small numbers: “Twice as many!” can also mean: two instead of one. Percentages without a base value say little.

INTERACTIVE · THE CLASS REPRESENTATIVE ELECTION

Change the votes with + and −. Proportion and angle are recalculated as you go.

EXAMPLE 7 · CALCULATING ANGLES

Election result out of 30 votes: Anna 12, Ben 8, Cem 6, Dana 4. Calculate the proportions and the angles for the pie chart.

Anna: $\tfrac{12}{30} = 40\%$ → $144^\circ$ · Ben: $\tfrac{8}{30} \approx 26.7\%$ → $96^\circ$

Cem: $20\%$ → $72^\circ$ · Dana: $\approx 13.3\%$ → $48^\circ$. Check: $144 + 96 + 72 + 48 = 360$

EXAMPLE 8 · PERCENTAGE POINTS

A newspaper says: “The proportion of cyclists rose from 20% to 25%.” By how much did it rise?

By $25 - 20 = 5$ percentage points. Relative to the old 20%: $\tfrac{5}{20} = 25\%$.

5 percentage points; that is a rise of 25%.

EXERCISES

Which angle in a pie chart belongs to a) 25%   b) 10%   c) 45%   d) 20%?

a) $90^\circ$   b) $36^\circ$   c) $162^\circ$   d) $72^\circ$

Draw a pie chart: sport 40%, reading 15%, music 25%, other 20%.

Angles: $144^\circ$, $54^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $72^\circ$. Together $360^\circ$.

24 people asked name their favourite colour: 6 red, 9 blue, 3 green, 6 yellow. Calculate the proportions and angles and draw a bar chart and a pie chart.

Red 25% ($90^\circ$), blue 37.5% ($135^\circ$), green 12.5% ($45^\circ$), yellow 25% ($90^\circ$).

Turnout at an election rose from 60% to 66%. By how many percentage points, and by what percentage?

By 6 percentage points. $\tfrac{6}{60} = 10\%$: by 10%.

A headline: “Accidents at the junction have doubled!” Last year there was one accident, this year two. What is correct about the headline, and what is misleading?

Correct: 2 is double 1, i.e. an increase of 100%. Misleading: with such small numbers it may be chance. Without the base values it sounds more dramatic than it is.

TEST YOURSELF!

Which angle belongs to 30%?

$30 \cdot 3.6^\circ = 108^\circ$

A sector has $54^\circ$. What percentage is that?

$54 \div 3.6 = 15$

A proportion rises from 40% to 50%. By how many percentage points?

10 percentage points (that is 25% more).

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

a) 15% of 240   b) What percentage is 27 out of 90?   c) 6% is €9. Base value?

a) 36   b) 30%   c) €150

Connecting with chapter 2.3: After a rise of 8% a book costs €54. Set up an equation and solve it.

$1.08 \cdot x = 54 \;\big|\; \div 1.08$ → $x = 50$. The book cost €50.

A tablet costs €400. There is a 10% discount and, for immediate payment, another 3% cash discount on the reduced price. How much do you pay?

$400 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.97 = €349.20$

Is 50% of 30 the same as 30% of 50? Check and give a general reason.

Both are 15. In general: $\tfrac{a}{100} \cdot b = \tfrac{a \cdot b}{100} = \tfrac{b}{100} \cdot a$, the commutative law.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

How the per cent sign came about

In the 15th century Italian merchants calculated a great deal with interest and profits “of a hundred”, in Italian per cento. Because they had to write it so often, they abbreviated it: first “p cento”, then “p c” with a little loop. This abbreviation can be seen in an Italian arithmetic manuscript from around 1425.

With fast writing the sign wore down. By around 1650 the loop already looked like a horizontal fraction bar with a circle above it and one below it. In the 19th century the bar tilted, and the “p” disappeared: % was finished. So the sign is not “divided by 100” but a worn-down abbreviation.

Source: F. Cajori, A History of Mathematical Notations, Volume I, Chicago 1928, section on the per cent sign.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

BASIC PROBLEMS

$W = p\% \cdot G$ · $p\% = \tfrac{W}{G}$ · $G = \tfrac{W}{p\%}$

35% of €80 = €28

EVERYDAY LIFE

Discount: old price minus reduction · gross = net + 19%

€250 net → €297.50 gross

BY AND TO

$p\%$ more: multiplier $1 + \tfrac{p}{100}$ · less: $1 - \tfrac{p}{100}$ · back: divide by the multiplier

€360 after a 20% discount: €450 before

CHARTS

Pie chart: $1\% \to 3.6^\circ$ · percentage points are not per cent

40% → 144°
